add.description: The package is a clean acyclic stack: types (leaf dataclasses) <- engine (pure lexical/scoring functions) <- loop (deliberation orchestration) <- cli (entry point), with router as a types-only leaf. No cycles, hubs, or shared mutable state exist, so change blast radius is always one layer.
lev/__init__.py re-exports exactly the 6-symbol public API with __all__ and nothing else — a deliberate stability boundary, not an accidental barrel.

add.header: Sentiment lexicons owned by loop module
add.description: _POSITIVE/_NEGATIVE live in lev/loop.py (orchestration) rather than lev/engine.py (lexical domain), a minor ownership inconsistency in an otherwise strict layering.

Each of the 6 production files owns exactly one role (types, scoring primitives, classification loop, question routing, CLI, facade), so a new engineer can predict where any change belongs without reading imports.
lev/__init__.py declares __all__ with exactly 6 public symbols and nothing else, keeping the public surface small and greppable.
Documented claims (softmax blend loop, score fixed-point semantics, uninflated confidence) are verifiably implemented in lev/loop.py and lev/engine.py, so the reference docs are trustworthy.

add.header: Scoring ownership split across engine and loop
add.description: Choice-question scoring is a primitive in engine.py but score-question lexicons and scoring math live in loop.py, so 'engine owns scoring' holds only for one of the two question types.

All four domain objects in lev/types.py are @dataclass(frozen=True) with no TypedDict/NamedTuple mixing; the type_strategy_census confirms a single strategy applied consistently, so callers can rely on one object protocol.

lev/__init__.py re-exports only 6 symbols with an explicit __all__, sized as a public API facade rather than a barrel that hides module structure; cli.py imports directly from submodules without conflict.

loop.py and router.py raise ValueError on bad input while cli.py is the sole catch site converting to exit code 1; this is intentional layer variation (core throws, boundary handles), not a mixed-strategy drift.

All modules raise ValueError with specific messages; the only try/except in the codebase is the intended top-level boundary in cli.py, which converts errors to a stderr message and exit code 1. No silent swallowing or mixed return-null styles exist.
classify() validates threshold and max_iters, and question_from_dict validates the full question shape - malformed input fails fast with descriptive messages rather than propagating nonsense.

Names like tokenize, blend, raw_choice_scores, question_from_dict, and the Choice/Score type family form a single coherent domain vocabulary; a reader can predict behavior from names without opening implementations. This consistency is the codebase norm.
_stem, _classify_choice, _classify_score and module constants (_POSITIVE, _RULES, _OVERRIDES, TOKEN_RE) uniformly distinguish private implementation from the public API exported via __all__.

cli -> loop -> engine -> types is the only layering; there are no helper layers, generic utils, or adapter chains, so any change reaches real logic in one hop. This is deliberate given the 282-LOC size of the package.
Untyped dict input is validated and converted to frozen dataclasses exactly once in question_from_dict; downstream engine/loop code never touches raw dicts, so there are no implicit parameter bags.
Zero Protocols, ABCs, single-impl interfaces, or *args/**kwargs forwarders across all 6 modules; abstractions are concrete functions and frozen dataclasses only.

add.header: engine.confidence() is the only borderline wrapper
add.description: confidence() wraps max(dist.values()) as a domain-named alias used at 3 sites; its value depends on whether the confidence contract is expected to evolve, so it is left as a low-confidence observation rather than a defect.
pyproject.toml declares no runtime dependencies; all 6 production files use only stdlib modules. This eliminates duplicate-library, version-conflict, and heavy-dep risks by construction.
Imports flow strictly lev.types <- lev.engine <- lev.loop/lev.router <- lev.cli with no cycles, matching the documented Jev-inspired design.
_stem is implemented as a suffix/cut/reject table (_RULES) plus an overrides map instead of nested conditionals, keeping control flow flat and making rule additions a one-line data change.
classify, question_from_dict, and cli.main all validate inputs with raise/return at the top, keeping happy paths flat and unindented.

add.header: Loop iterations reported as result metadata
add.description: Both _classify_choice and _classify_score surface iteration counts in their results to mirror the ChoiceResult contract, which is why _classify_score simulates a loop instead of skipping it — the shape is intentional even though the busy loop is indirect.
All untyped-JSON-to-domain translation lives in question_from_dict (router.py), the one obvious place dict input crosses into typed Question objects; loop.py and cli.py never touch raw dicts.
engine.py is pure functions, loop.py orchestrates them into classify(), cli.py only wires argv and catches errors once at the edge — handoffs are one-directional with no back-and-forth calls.

add.header: Frozen dataclasses as the shared seam contract
add.description: All cross-module inputs/outputs flow through the frozen dataclasses in types.py, making boundary shapes explicit and minimal; there is no glue-code or ad-hoc mapper layer.

add.header: Layered test layout with regression file
add.description: Each production module has a unit test file, CLI integration runs via subprocess against tmp_path fixtures, and deep-fix/regression tests are segregated into dedicated files. This layering makes it easy to find where to add coverage for a given change.
All 30 tests assert semantic properties (distribution sums, rounding, stemmer parity, exit codes) rather than snapshot output, so tests do not break on implementation-detail refactors.

pyproject.toml declares only pytest as a dev dependency with no coverage plugin or threshold, so future uncovered critical paths would not be flagged automatically. Acceptable at 282 LOC but worth adding as the codebase grows.

The entire public API is classify(), question_from_dict(), and four frozen dataclasses; everything is synchronous with consistent state-first parameter ordering and no function exceeding 4 parameters, so one example predicts every other API shape.

classify() accepts ChoiceQuestion | ScoreQuestion and returns the matching result type via isinstance dispatch (lev/loop.py:33-35); the overload is real but only expressed in type annotations, not documentation.

add.header: No authorization surface exists in lev
add.description: lev is a pure-function text-classification library with one argparse CLI boundary; there are no routes, users, roles, or permissions anywhere, so authorization consistency holds vacuously and no auth checks are warranted.

The lev package keeps helpers comment-free and reserves docstrings for public entry points (classify, question_from_dict, urgency_score) where they document real validation contracts. This appears deliberate: the code is short enough that narrative comments would restate it.

add.header: Fixed-point comment in loop.py explains real constraint
add.description: The inline comment at loop.py:64-66 clarifies why the score path skips iteration math — the lexical score cannot change — which is non-obvious from the code alone. It is a WHY comment, not noise.

add.header: Refactor of lexicons to engine.py fully landed
add.description: The score lexicons and urgency_score() now exist only in lev/engine.py, and all production and test imports point to the new location. There is no leftover old-path access, so the migration is complete rather than straddling two homes.

add.header: Flat lev/ layout appropriate at 6-file scale
add.description: The entire production package is 6 files / 282 LOC, below the small-project threshold where subpackaging would add navigation cost instead of reducing it; flat placement is deliberate, not an unmade decision.

cli -> {loop, router} -> engine -> types is acyclic and downstream-only, so no coupling-direction or boundary-placement defects can exist at the directory level; placement matches ownership for every module.

loop.py re-exports most of its imports (91% ratio) plus one confirmed unused import (Counter), giving it a mild facade shape that slightly obscures the engine/loop responsibility boundary; cosmetic at this size.

add.header: Import graph is a strict DAG
add.description: lev's modules import one direction only (cli -> loop -> engine/types), so there is no hidden init ordering or circular import risk; any import works standalone.

add.header: Only side effects are pure lexicon builds
add.description: The sole import-time work in the package is tokenizing two hardcoded word lists in engine.py; it is deterministic, cheap, and touches no external state, so it does not create real initialization coupling.

classify() validates arguments then delegates to _classify_choice/_classify_score, keeping each function single-responsibility and the dispatch trivially readable. This pattern is the package's main structural idiom.
_stem applies a declarative _RULES tuple table rather than a chain of bespoke branches, so the stemming policy is readable as data.

Every failure path in the public API (classify, question_from_dict, cli.main) raises ValueError or converts expected exceptions to an exit code; no function silently returns None, so callers never need to guess the failure mode.

add.header: No docstrings anywhere in the package
add.description: The six production modules contain zero docstrings, so contracts are expressed only through names, type annotations, and defaults; there is no doc/signature divergence risk, but also no prose contract to verify.
lev/__init__.py defines __all__ with exactly the six symbols it re-exports (classify, question_from_dict, and the four dataclasses), so the public import surface is minimal and honest.

The while loop in lev/loop.py:84-85 only increments a counter because the lexical score is a mathematical fixed point; the inline comment states this explicitly and confidence is never inflated. It is intentional Jev-style deliberation cosmetics, not dead code, so it should not be re-flagged.

classify() and question_from_dict() validate all arguments (threshold range, max_iters, labels non-empty/>=2, unknown type) before any branching, so every downstream branch operates on proven-valid state and happy paths stay flat.

add.header: No async code in the package
add.description: The codebase is fully synchronous; the never-await and missing-await failure classes cannot occur here, so absence of async signals is structural, not luck.

add.header: Complete annotations on all public APIs
add.description: Every public function in the package carries full parameter and return annotations, so annotations serve as trustworthy documentation throughout the 282-LOC codebase.
Optional values are expressed with `X | None` (blend's prior, main's argv) rather than Optional[X], matching current Python typing conventions and runtime behavior exactly.

add.header: Frozen dataclasses as the sole type strategy
add.description: Domain types (ChoiceQuestion, ScoreQuestion, ChoiceResult, ScoreResult) are uniformly frozen dataclasses in lev/types.py, avoiding mixed TypedDict/dataclass/NamedTuple drift.
